summary: Store strings in a tree of characters so that shared prefixes are shared nodes, enabling fast prefix search, autocomplete, and word lookup.
lesson: A trie stores a set of strings as a tree of characters, where any two words sharing a prefix also share the tree nodes for that prefix. Looking up a word or checking whether any word starts with a given prefix costs only O(L), where L is the length of the word or prefix being checked -- completely independent of how many words are stored, unlike scanning a word list. This makes it the right structure whenever a problem needs repeated prefix queries (autocomplete, dictionary word search) against a fixed or growing set of strings. The key structural detail is the is_word flag on each node -- it's what distinguishes "this prefix exists" from "this exact word was inserted."
recognize_when: Problem involves a dictionary of words plus prefix queries (starts-with, autocomplete)
You need to repeatedly search for words or prefixes among a large, static or growing set of strings
Word search on a grid/board combined with a dictionary of valid words
Naive approach would re-scan the whole word list for every prefix check
Building a word/phone-number/IP structure where common prefixes should be deduplicated

complexity.notes: Insert/search/startsWith each cost O(L) where L is the word length, independent of how many words are stored; space is O(N*L) in the worst case (alphabet size branching factor per node) but shared prefixes reduce this in practice.

gotchas: Confusing search() (must end on a complete word, is_word True) with starts_with() (just needs the path to exist)
Not marking is_word=True at the end of insert, so search always returns False even for inserted words
Using a fixed-size array of 26 children when the alphabet isn't guaranteed lowercase a-z; a dict is safer and more general
